title: Phones
hook: the phone can pull us from the present
tomorrow: a clip that would blow up online. post it or not?

segments.voice: Yesterday, silence, argued from two sides: keep it, as Elijah did, or speak and sing, as the Council asked. Both live in one paragraph, and the question is which time is now. The line was room to speak.

A taco truck, two friends talking again after a hard week, and a phone face up on the table. It lights up. A glance. It lights up again. Nothing urgent, just the pull, like a tap on the shoulder from somewhere else. Even a glance changes the table. Luke tells of a house with the same tug-of-war. Jesus is a guest at the home of two sisters. One sits at his feet and listens. The other is everywhere at once.
screen: `A PHONE FACE UP.` → `A TAP FROM SOMEWHERE ELSE.` → `TWO SISTERS, ONE GUEST.`

segments.voice: Luke says Martha "was busy about much serving." Good work, real welcome. But she's pulled in so many directions she can't sit with the guest she's serving, and she complains that her sister isn't helping. Jesus answers gently, in the Douay-Rheims Bible: "Martha, Martha, thou art careful, and art troubled about many things: But one thing is necessary." Careful, in that older English, means full of care. Anxious. Many things, pulling at once. A phone is many things in one pocket: every chat, every feed, every place but this one. Jesus says something similar about time: "Be not therefore solicitous for to morrow; for the morrow will be solicitous for itself." Solicitous is another old word for anxious. A French Jesuit, Jean-Pierre de Caussade, is remembered for a phrase Catholics still use: the sacrament of the present moment, the idea that God meets a person in the moment they're actually in. Not the next notification. This one. The person across the table exists in this moment; the feed will still be there in an hour. The point isn't that a phone is evil; nothing in these texts says that. It's that attention goes one place at a time, and Mary chose to give hers to the one in front of her.
screen: `ONE SITS, ONE IS EVERYWHERE.` · `TROUBLED ABOUT MANY THINGS.` · `NOT SOLICITOUS FOR TOMORROW.` · `THE SACRAMENT OF THE PRESENT MOMENT.` · then, large: `HERE, NOW.`

segments.voice: Put your phone in another room, or out of reach. Walk slowly for a minute, even just across the room and back, and notice what's here: the floor under your feet, one sound, one color you hadn't seen. When your hand drifts toward the pocket out of habit, let it hang open instead. Let the room be enough for that minute.
Phones. A tool that can carry a person anywhere but here: Martha's many things, folded into one pocket.
Your line: here, now. One thing is necessary, and it's usually already in the room. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Some Catholic families keep phones away at meals and during prayer, and some Catholics fast from screens in Lent; the Church speaks of meeting God in the present moment of ordinary life.

fork.setup: your little sister is telling you about her day while you scroll. she stops mid-story. what would Mary in Luke's story do?
options: put the phone out of reach and ask her to start over.
say 'keep going, I'm listening' and keep scrolling.
finish the video first, then give her full attention.
fork.reveal: Mary sat and heard; Martha, troubled about many things, couldn't. here, now means the phone out of reach, and the person first.
